claims.claim: The government should tighten rent control on subdivided units through tenure security and a band-based cap on initial rents, not a hard cap on rent levels.
A hard cap on rent levels would help current tenants but shrink future supply and fail the most vulnerable households.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped rent increases within existing tenancies but left initial rents unregulated and excluded co-living SDUs.
Real rent burden for SDU households worsened from 31% to 34% even under the ordinance.
The long-run elasticity of marginal SDU-type supply is estimated at 0.31 to 0.48, meaning a 10% cap-induced rent reduction removes 3-5% of stock over five years.
A 15% cut in initial rents would transfer about 900 dollars per month to incumbents while leaving 3,000-4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment.
The households excluded by a hard cap are precisely the vulnerable populations: new arrivals, single-parent households, and public-housing waiters.
Berlin's Mietendeckel caused measurable supply contraction within a year, and when it was lifted, suppressed rent increases released above the pre-cap trend.
New York's second-generation rent control scheme shows modest contraction because it is light on first-rent regulation.
First-generation controls on rent levels contract stock, while second-generation controls on increases do not.
The stable stock under the 2021 ordinance is an artifact of a non-binding instrument and does not indicate behavior under a binding cap.
Enforcement capacity covers under 6% of stock annually, and a band-based register would require 40-60 staff-years to establish.
A complaint-driven enforcement regime would miss the tenants least able to complain, such as those without written agreements and newest arrivals.
No design was identified under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last.

The landlords' association claims members will exit if returns fall below mortgage cost, but it has no data on actual margins and its compliance-cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34% response rate.
Exit of landlords is real but modest under light regulation, and larger under binding caps.
61% of tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security, and 74% for a faster public-housing offer.
The binding constraint for SDU tenants is queue length and insecurity, not price alone.
A workable middle path is to cap initial rent by reference to a published, indexed per-square-foot band, defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation.
The government should tighten tenure security immediately, build the band infrastructure, expand the public-housing queue, and not cap the first rent.

Those excluded are precisely the population named in D1: new arrivals, single-parent households, public-housing waiters [D1p2].
